newsitem.title: USA: CUC, iQVC say bigger is better in online shopping.
newsitem.headline: CUC, iQVC say bigger is better in online shopping.

text.p: The predominately female shoppers who frequent iQVC's Web site soon can enlist the aid of an online fashion consultant to choose clothes and jewelry best suited to their figure and face.

Subscribers to CUC International's new netMarket Web site (http://www.netmarket.com) can bid on merchandise in weekly live auctions, hunt for bargains at a continuing flea market and earn frequent-shopper points for every purchase they make.
The innovations are just a few features the two online retailers are offering to ensure a steady stream of customers walks through their virtual thresholds.

Clever technology aside, companies such as QVC (http://www.iqvc.com) and CUC have a better chance than many of making it as online retailers because of their low costs, established brand names, well-oiled order taking and shipping procedures, and their sense of community, according to a recent online retailing report.

According to the "Internet Retail" report compiled by analysts at investment banker Morgan Stanley, online shopping is likely to go through a "boomlet-bust-boom" cycle that will weed out all but the strongest contenders. Survivors will include well-managed companies with recognised Web brands or big retailers that take the Internet plunge, according to the report.

Today's most popular Internet shopping sites sell everything from software to greeting cards. In May, the 10 most popular shopping sites, according to Web auditor PC Meter, included four stores selling or giving away software -- download.com (http://www.download.com), shareware.com (http://www.shareware.com), Hot-Files.com (http://www.hotfiles.com) and Jumbo.com (http://www.jumbo.com) -- as well as bookseller Amazon.com (http://www.amazon.com), music seller Columbia House (http://www.columbiahouse.com) and greeting-card maker Blue Mountain Arts (http://www.bluemountainarts.com).

CUC and iQVC eventually want to count themselves in that number. In May, iQVC was one of the top 25 online stores and CUC's corporate Web site, CUC.com, made it into the top 40, according to PC Meter's Doug McFarland.

CUC is placing bets on netMarket, a Web superstore the Stamford, Conn., membership buying group launched recently that combines merchandise from several existing CUC sites, including Shoppers Advantage, Travel Advantage, AutoVantage and Book Stacks Unlimited. CUC will continue to operate those sites but will only accept new members through netMarket. Anyone can shop on netMarket, but customers who buy a $69 annual membership receive additional discounts and other bonuses.
CUC wants netMarket to become the warehouse club of the Internet, said Scott Melland, a CUC interactive services vice president.
"By bringing together our services, we're overwhelming people with a lot of value. That will lead us to be much more successful on the Web," Melland said.
In addition to netMarket, in June, CUC paid America Online $50 million to secure prime advertising real estate on the No. 1 online service.

CUC hopes its actions will boost the number of members who shop online, and ultimately membership sales, which is where the company makes its money. Currently, CUC counts 350,000 members who shop online compared with 68 million who use the company's 20-year-old mail-order division.

CUC expects online shoppers to spend an estimated $1 billion this year; best-selling products including computer products, home electronics, office equipment, vacation packages, and free new-car summaries.
At iQVC in West Chester, Pa., one of the most popular times to shop is midnight, when the new daily best buy is announced simultaneously online and on TV.
"We do a very big weekend business and we do a big lunch business. I think people are checking in from work," said iQVC General Manager Stuart Spiegel.

Introduced in September 1996, iQVC has grown to about 350,000 page views a month or about 1 million "hits." iQVC is turning a profit on monthly revenue of more than $1 million. That's peanuts compared with QVC's $2 billion TV home shopping network, but it's premature to compare the two, Spiegel said.
"It's like comparing a new store for Bloomingdale's against the whole chain," he said. "Until the Internet becomes a mass medium and over half the people in the country use it, it won't be that big."
According to Spiegel, iQVC's Web site will be redesigned by summer's end to accommodate the latest Web browsers from Netscape and Microsoft and offer more personalization.

The "My Style Advisor" fashion consultant falls into the latter category, as does an e-mail notification service that lets shoppers with special interests know when merchandise they might like goes on sale. Coming in September: a search function that lets shoppers hunt for products by brand name, price or feature. The site already hosts live chats and public message boards, two popular community-building devices.
"We have a robust community, but that's not why we're doing well," Spiegel said. "What's important is good old-fashioned retailing: deliver what you say, when you say, at a valuable price."
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
